newsitem.title: IRAQ: Greece sends diplomat to reopen its embassy in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Greece sends diplomat to reopen its embassy in Iraq.

text.p: Greece has sent a diplomat to reopen its embassy in Iraq, closed down since the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.
"The (Greek) embassy will be fully operated," Christos Skoursis, newly appointed Greek charge d'affaires, told Reuters on Wednesday.
Greece along with other Western countries closed down their diplomatic missions in Baghdad after the 1991 U.S.-led Gulf War which ejected Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
Skoursis said the embassy would be opened after settling some procedures. "There are certain matters that we have to settle before opening the embassy," he said without elaborating.
In Athens, a foreign ministry spokesman said the embassy would be run by the charge d'affaires and there were no immediate plans to send an ambassador to Iraq.

Several Western countries have reopened either interest sections or embassies in Baghdad since its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations went into effect in December. The Iraqi News Agency (INA) said Skoursis arrived in Baghdad following a decision taken last month by the Greek foreign ministry to reopen its embassy in Iraq.
It said Under-Secretary of the Iraqi Foreign Ministry Abdul- Jabbar al-Douri visited Greece in April and met with its foreign minister and other officials.
INA said Skoursis had worked in his country's embassy in Iraq from 1976 until 1980.

The deal with the U.N. allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and medicines for Iraqis, suffering from U.N. sanctions imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of the emirate.
Last month Italy and Spain sent diplomats to reopen their missions in Baghdad. France has had a charge d'affaires in Iraq since 1995.
